metadata.title: MCP Builder.
metadata.purpose: Answer whether building an MCP server starts with code or research, using the mcp-builder skill's own tool-naming convention (github_create_issue vs github_list_repos) as the concrete case. Lands the carry-out that tool quality is measured by proven task completion, not endpoint coverage, and that proof only reaches as far as read-only calls.
metadata.anchor_pair: B02 -> B03 (github_create_issue vs github_list_repos: same naming pattern, one a write, one read-only; only the read-only one fits the ten-question, read-only evaluation proof directly)

beats.narration_text: Someone asks how to write an MCP server for GitHub. But mcp-builder starts with research, not code — study the protocol, pick a language, plan the tool list first. What does that cover?

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'How do I write an MCP server for GitHub?', hesitates on 'write', corrects to 'research and build', lands the real question

props.text:

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('write' -> 'research and build') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: Research means three things before any code: read the actual MCP protocol spec, pick a language — TypeScript with Zod is recommended — and plan the tool list against the target API's own documentation. When those docs are live, that plan is grounded in the API's real shape. When they're offline or stale, the research phase has nothing solid to plan from, and stalls.

shot.new_visual_element: A code-editor icon jumping straight to 'implement', crossed out; the real order RESEARCH -> IMPLEMENT -> REVIEW -> EVALUATE; RESEARCH expands into protocol / language / tool list; docs-live vs docs-stale branching

production_viz.label: Research first, or it stalls
production_viz.mechanic: A ghost card 'jump to code' fades in center, gets a terracotta strike, dissolves. Four cards appear left to right: RESEARCH, IMPLEMENT, REVIEW, EVALUATE, connected by arrows, RESEARCH outlined in teal. RESEARCH expands downward into three labelled sub-cards: protocol spec, language (TypeScript + Zod), tool list. Then the API-docs source branches: a 'docs: live' path lights the tool-list card teal and it fills in; a 'docs: offline/stale' path reaches the same tool-list card and it stays empty, dimmed, with a small terracotta 'stalls' label.

beats.narration_text: Every tool carries four things: an input schema — Zod in TypeScript, Pydantic in Python — typed and constrained, with a description on each field; an output schema, so the client knows the shape of what comes back; four annotations — read-only, destructive, idempotent, open-world; and an error message that names the problem and suggests the fix. Names follow one pattern, prefix then action: github, underscore, create, underscore, issue — a write. Github, underscore, list, underscore, repos — read-only.

shot.new_visual_element: Four tool-anatomy cards; THE ANCHOR -- github_create_issue and github_list_repos built segment by segment, one tagged WRITE, one tagged READ-ONLY

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR — one pattern, two tools
production_viz.mechanic: Four cards fade in in sequence: input schema (Zod/Pydantic), output schema, four annotation chips (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, openWorldHint), error message. All four fade out. THE ANCHOR. 'github_create_issue' builds left to right in monospace, segment by segment (github_ / create_ / issue), each segment briefly highlighted terracotta as it's named (prefix / action-verb / action-object), then settles black with a WRITE chip in terracotta beside it. Beneath, 'github_list_repos' builds the same way, settling with a READ-ONLY chip in teal beside it. THESE TWO STRINGS RETURN AT B03.

beats.narration_text: Here's the both-directions of the evaluation rule. github_list_repos is read-only — call it, check the answer against the real list, done. It fits the ten-question proof directly. github_create_issue writes real state, an actual issue gets created. Since the standard requires read-only, verifiable questions, a task built around create_issue can't be one of the ten — even though it's exactly the call an agent gets asked to make. Same asymmetry in the stack: TypeScript with Zod is recommended, even for a team that knows Python better.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- list_repos fires into a lit 'checked' card; create_issue fires into a card marked 'writes state -- outside the ten'; a small TypeScript/Python asymmetry note beneath

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — checked vs outside the ten
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 STRINGS RETURN, identical. 'github_list_repos' fires an arrow into a teal card reading 'checked against real list ✓'. 'github_create_issue' fires an arrow into a different card reading 'writes real state' which then gets a dashed border and a label 'outside the ten' — no strike, just excluded. Beneath both, a small two-column note fades in: 'TypeScript + Zod' on the left under a checkmark, 'team knows Python' on the right under a plain dash — same recommend-anyway shape as the tool split above.

beats.narration_text: A good MCP server isn't judged by how many endpoints it covers — it's judged by real tasks it can prove it completes. And that proof only reaches as far as read-only calls, checked directly against the real answer.

props.quote: A good MCP server isn't judged by how many endpoints it covers — it's judged by real tasks it can prove it completes. And that proof only reaches as far as read-only calls, checked directly against the real answer.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — read it with me: Build an MCP server for the OpenWeatherMap API. Use TypeScript and Zod. Cover current weather, forecasts, and historical data. Follow the mcp-builder skill. Watch whether Claude starts with research — the protocol, the API's docs — before writing any code. Then check each tool for a Zod input schema, an output schema, and the four annotations: read-only, destructive, idempotent, open-world. Liam, in for Bear.
